question: In the 'Mini Frontier LLM' capstone of an LLM research engineer course, what is a research engineer said to be judged on?
options: The size of the largest model they have personally pretrained end to end
Mastery of a single component, such as attention kernels or tokenizers
How many production frameworks they can configure without reading the code
Making the whole pipeline run, produce a number, and be reproduced
explanation: The capstone frames the job as end-to-end: make the whole pipeline run, get a reproducible number out of it, and let others reproduce it. Knowing one component in depth is not enough if the pieces can't be wired together. Model size and framework familiarity are not the criteria.

question: What sequence of artifacts does the 'Mini Frontier LLM' capstone pipeline produce, starting from raw text?
options: GPT, tokenizer, pretrained model, preference-aligned model, evaluation number, instruction-tuned model, reasoning policy
Tokenizer, GPT, pretrained model, eval number, instruction-tuned model, preference-aligned model, RLVR reasoning policy
Tokenizer, reward model, pretrained model, reasoning policy, instruction-tuned model, evaluation number, aligned model
Pretrained model, tokenizer, instruction-tuned model, evaluation number, GPT, preference-aligned model, reasoning policy
explanation: The order follows the data dependencies: you need a tokenizer before a GPT can see ids, a pretrained model before you can evaluate or fine-tune it, SFT before preference alignment, and the RLVR reasoning stage on top. Each module solves a problem created by the one before it. The scrambled orders break those dependencies (e.g. a GPT cannot be built before its vocabulary is fixed).

question: On what hardware is the tiny end-to-end version of the 'Mini Frontier LLM' capstone designed to run?
options: A free cloud TPU, in about ten minutes
An 8-GPU node, in roughly a day
A single A100 GPU, in about an hour
A laptop CPU, in roughly 20 seconds
explanation: The driver code/scripts/capstone.py runs a tiny version of the pipeline on CPU in under about 20 seconds with less than 1 GB of RAM and 0 GPU-hours. The point is to see every stage work on hardware you already own; the GPU-scale numbers are for scaling each stage up later.

question: In the capstone pipeline diagram, which stage feeds the held-out perplexity measurement?
options: The evaluation harness, applied to the pretrained model
The DPO stage, applied to the chosen/rejected preference pairs
The GRPO stage, applied to the verifiable arithmetic rewards
The BPE tokenizer, applied to the raw held-out corpus
explanation: Held-out perplexity comes from the evaluation harness run on the model coming out of the pretraining loop. It is the pretraining metric. DPO and GRPO are later post-training stages, and the tokenizer only produces ids; none of them yields perplexity.

question: Which optimizer setup does the capstone's pretraining loop use?
options: SGD with Nesterov momentum and a step-decay learning-rate schedule
AdamW with a cosine learning-rate schedule and gradient clipping
Lion with linear warmup, EMA weight averaging, and no clipping
Adafactor with a constant learning rate and no gradient clipping
explanation: The pipeline diagram labels the pretraining loop 'AdamW + cosine LR + clip': a cosine-warmup learning rate, AdamW steps, and global gradient-norm clipping. These are the components built in the optimization modules (llmre.optim.adamw, schedule, clip). The other optimizers are not part of the llmre pretraining loop.

question: In the capstone pipeline, what comes after SFT on the path to alignment?
options: LoRA, then preference data, then DPO or reward-model-plus-PPO
Perplexity evaluation, then MinHash deduplication of the SFT data
Tokenizer retraining on chat data, then pretraining from scratch
Tool use, then new BPE merges, then ablations on the merged vocab
explanation: After response-masked SFT, the pipeline adds LoRA for cheap fine-tuning, then preference data, then either DPO or the classic reward-model + PPO route. Only after that comes GRPO + RLVR, reasoning, tool use and agents. Retraining the tokenizer or re-pretraining are not post-SFT steps.

question: What is the final deliverable at the bottom of the capstone pipeline diagram?
options: A deployed chat endpoint serving the model
A leaderboard submission on a public benchmark
A merged LoRA checkpoint uploaded to a model hub
Ablations leading to a written experiment report
explanation: The diagram ends with 'ablations -> a written experiment report'. The course stresses that the deliverable is not the model itself but a report a colleague can reproduce. Deployment, leaderboards and checkpoint uploads are not part of the capstone pipeline.

question: Where does the code for the 'Mini Frontier LLM' capstone live?
options: In a set of independent notebooks, one per module, with no shared package between them
In one coherent package under code/src/llmre/, built up across earlier modules
Inside Hugging Face Transformers, configured entirely through YAML files
In a fresh standalone repository written from scratch only for the capstone
explanation: The whole codebase is one package, llmre, under code/src/llmre/. The capstone is a guided tour of that package as a project, not new code written from scratch. It does not rely on HF Transformers or disconnected notebooks.

question: Which script runs the tiny end-to-end capstone pipeline and writes a filled-in experiment report?
options: code/scripts/bench_attention.py
code/experiments/scaling_sweep.py
code/tests/test_capstone.py
code/scripts/capstone.py
explanation: code/scripts/capstone.py is the driver: it runs a tiny version of the stages on CPU and writes code/reports/capstone_report.md. scaling_sweep.py is the scaling/ablation experiment, bench_attention.py benchmarks attention, and test_capstone.py is the smoke test that asserts the learning signals.

question: What is the main point of the capstone, given that it is built from code written in Modules 0-19?
options: To see the existing code work end to end and know how each stage scales
To replace the earlier from-scratch modules with optimized kernels
To rewrite every component from scratch with production frameworks
To introduce a new architecture not covered in earlier modules
explanation: The capstone is explicitly not new code you must write from scratch; it assembles what you already wrote and runs it as one pipeline. The goal is to watch it work end to end and understand how each stage scales up. It does not replace or rewrite the earlier modules.

question: In byte-level BPE training, what is the starting vocabulary before any merges?
options: The 26 lowercase letters plus punctuation
The 50,257 tokens of the GPT-2 vocabulary
All Unicode code points that appear in the corpus
The 256 raw byte values
explanation: Byte-level BPE starts from the 256 possible byte values and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new id. Because any string is a sequence of bytes, nothing is ever out-of-vocabulary. Starting from Unicode code points or letters would leave unseen characters unrepresentable.

question: Why is nothing ever out-of-vocabulary for a byte-level BPE tokenizer?
options: Unknown words are mapped to a special <unk> token that is added during BPE training
Every string is a sequence of bytes, and all 256 byte values are in the base vocab
Rare characters are dropped before encoding, so only symbols seen in training remain
The tokenizer retrains its merges on any new text it sees at encode time
explanation: Since the base vocabulary contains all 256 bytes, any input can always fall back to single-byte tokens. That is also why decode(encode(s)) == s holds exactly. An <unk> token or dropping characters would break that round-trip, and BPE does not retrain at encode time.

question: Which round-trip property should a byte-level BPE tokenizer satisfy for any string s?
options: encode(s) == sorted(encode(s))
decode(encode(s)) == s
encode(decode(s)) == s
len(encode(s)) == len(s)
explanation: Byte-level BPE is lossless: encoding a string and decoding the ids gives back exactly the same string. Token count is generally smaller than character count after merges, so the length equality is false. encode(decode(s)) mixes up types (s is a string, decode takes ids).

question: In llmre's BPETokenizer, what is described as 'the whole subtlety' of encoding?
options: Applying merges in random order to regularize the tokenizer
Applying the learned merges in the order they were learned
Applying the longest available merge first, regardless of order
Applying merges in alphabetical order of the byte pairs
explanation: The merges are stored as an ordered dict of (a, b) -> new_id, and encode must apply them in learned order. Later merges may depend on tokens created by earlier ones, so reordering produces different (wrong) tokenizations. Alphabetical, longest-first or random orders do not reproduce training.

question: How does llmre's BPETokenizer store its learned merges?
options: As an ordered dict mapping a pair (a, b) to a new id
As a set of strings with no ordering
As a trie of whole words learned from the corpus
As a matrix of pair frequencies recomputed on each encode
explanation: merges is an ordered dict of (a, b) -> new_id. The ordering matters because encode applies merges in the order they were learned. A set would lose that order, and recomputing frequencies at encode time is not how BPE encoding works.

question: What are the main components of the decoder-only GPT in llmre.model.gpt.GPT?
options: Token + positional embeddings, pre-norm blocks (causal attention + MLP), a final norm, a tied lm_head
An encoder stack, a decoder stack with cross-attention to the encoder output, and an untied output layer
Only token embeddings, a single shared attention layer, and a separate classifier per position
Convolutional embeddings, post-norm blocks with bidirectional attention, and a softmax output head
explanation: The capstone GPT is decoder-only: token and positional embeddings, a stack of pre-norm blocks each containing causal multi-head attention and an MLP, a final norm, and an lm_head tied to the token embedding. There is no encoder or cross-attention, and attention is causal, not bidirectional.

question: In llmre's GPT, what does forward(idx, targets) return?
options: Only the loss as a scalar
Only the sampled next token ids
A tuple (hidden_states, attention_weights)
A tuple (logits, loss)
explanation: forward(idx, targets) returns both the logits and the cross-entropy loss. Sampling is done separately by generate(...). Returning hidden states or attention weights is not the interface described.

question: What does weight tying mean in llmre's GPT?
options: The token embedding matrix and the lm_head weight are the same tensor
Every transformer block shares one set of attention and MLP weights
The query and key projections share a single weight matrix in each head
The positional and token embeddings are summed into one shared table
explanation: Weight tying means transformer.wte.weight is lm_head.weight: the same parameter maps ids to vectors at the input and vectors to logits at the output. It saves vocab_size x n_embd parameters. Sharing weights across blocks or between Q and K is a different (and not used) idea.

question: What scaled residual initialization standard deviation does llmre's GPT use for residual projections?
options: 0.02 * sqrt(2 * n_layer)
1 / sqrt(n_embd * n_layer)
0.02 / sqrt(2 * n_layer)
explanation: Residual projections are initialized with std 0.02 / sqrt(2 * n_layer). Each block adds two residual contributions (attention and MLP), so there are 2 * n_layer additions; scaling by 1/sqrt of that keeps the residual stream's variance from growing with depth. Multiplying by sqrt(n_layer) would do the opposite.

question: In llmre's GPT, which object fixes every tensor shape of the model?
options: The training loop's TrainConfig
The tokenizer's merges dictionary
The GPTConfig dataclass
The capstone report template
explanation: GPTConfig (llmre.model.config) holds n_layer, n_head, n_embd, block_size, vocab_size and so on, which determine every tensor shape. TrainConfig controls the optimization loop, not model shapes. The tokenizer influences vocab_size only indirectly by being passed into the config.

question: What objective does the capstone's pretraining stage minimize?
options: Binary cross-entropy of a real-vs-fake classifier
Mean squared error between embeddings of adjacent tokens
Negative reward from a learned reward model
Cross-entropy of the true next token at each position
explanation: Pretraining is next-token prediction: for each position, minimize the cross-entropy of the actual next token under the model's predicted distribution. MSE on embeddings or discriminator losses are not language-model pretraining objectives, and reward models belong to post-training.

question: In what order does the llmre pretraining loop's inner step act?
options: Forward/backward, AdamW step, then clip the gradients after the update has already been applied to the weights
Set the LR from the cosine-warmup schedule, forward/backward, clip the global grad norm, AdamW step
AdamW step, then forward/backward, then clip the grad norm, then set the LR for the next step
Clip the grad norm, set the LR from the schedule, AdamW step, then forward/backward last
explanation: The loop writes the learning rate for the current step, runs forward and backward to get gradients, clips the global gradient norm, then takes the AdamW step. Clipping must happen after backward and before the optimizer step; clipping after the step has no effect on that update.

question: What does gradient accumulation let the llmre pretraining loop do?
options: Reach a large effective batch size while fitting in small memory
Store the AdamW moment buffers in lower precision to save memory
Skip the backward pass on most micro-batches to save compute
Use a much higher learning rate safely without any warmup phase
explanation: Gradient accumulation sums gradients over several micro-batches before one optimizer step, so the effective batch is large while each forward/backward only holds one micro-batch in memory. It still requires a backward pass on every micro-batch, and it is unrelated to warmup or optimizer precision.

question: Which llmre modules does the training loop llmre.training.loop.train build on?
options: llmre.tools.registry.ToolRegistry, llmre.agents.react.run_react and llmre.reasoning.cot.cot_prompt
llmre.data.minhash, llmre.data.contamination and llmre.data.quality, applied per training batch
llmre.optim.adamw.AdamW, llmre.optim.schedule.cosine_warmup_lr and llmre.optim.clip.clip_grad_norm_
llmre.sft.lora.LoRALinear, llmre.preference.dpo.dpo_loss and llmre.rl.grpo.grpo_advantages
explanation: The pretraining loop is assembled from the from-scratch optimizer (AdamW), learning-rate schedule (cosine warmup) and gradient-norm clipping. LoRA/DPO/GRPO are post-training, tools/agents are later modules, and the data-quality modules feed the corpus rather than the loop.

question: How does the llmre data pipeline turn documents into training data?
options: Re-tokenize a random document at every step, truncate it to block_size, and pad shorter ones
Encode each document once, concatenate into one id stream with end-of-text ids, cut random (x, y) windows
Pad every document to the longest one in the corpus and train on each padded document separately
Shuffle all tokens globally across documents and sample them independently for each batch
explanation: pack_documents encodes everything once into a single id stream with end-of-text separators, and get_batch cuts random fixed-length windows. Packing avoids padding waste. Re-tokenizing every step wastes compute, and globally shuffling tokens destroys the sequences the model must learn.

question: In llmre's get_batch, how is the target window y related to the input window x?
options: y is x with 15% of tokens masked
y is x shifted left by one position
y is x reversed along the time axis
y is the same as x, position by position
explanation: Each target is the next token of the input at the same position, so y is x shifted by one. That single shift is the whole supervision signal for next-token prediction. Masking is BERT-style pretraining, and y == x would teach the model to copy its input.

question: Besides packing and batching, what must a data pipeline do at real scale?
options: Remove every repeated token within each document
Filter, deduplicate and decontaminate the corpus
Translate all documents into a single language
Sort the documents alphabetically before packing
explanation: At real scale the data pipeline is also where you filter low-quality text, deduplicate (e.g. with MinHash) and decontaminate against evaluation sets (llmre.data.quality, minhash, contamination). Translation, alphabetical sorting or removing repeated tokens are not standard pipeline steps.

question: What does the llmre.data.contamination module address in the data pipeline?
options: Balancing the mix of code, prose, and math in the training corpus by domain weights
Fixing invalid UTF-8 byte sequences so the byte-level tokenizer does not fail on them
Removing eval-set content from the training corpus so benchmark scores are not inflated
Detecting malware and phishing pages embedded in web-crawled documents before training starts
explanation: Decontamination removes overlap between the training corpus and evaluation benchmarks; otherwise the model may have seen test items and score artificially high. It sits next to quality filtering and MinHash deduplication in the data-quality tooling. It is not about malware, encoding or domain mixing.

question: How does the memory of standard (non-Flash) attention grow with sequence length T?
options: As T^2, because it materializes a T x T score matrix per head
As T^3, because of the cost of the T x T by T x d matrix multiply
Linearly in T, because each token stores one key and one value vector
Logarithmically in T, because softmax normalization compresses the scores
explanation: Standard attention builds the full T x T score matrix per head, so memory grows quadratically with T. FlashAttention computes the same result in tiles without ever storing that matrix. The matmul cost is T^2 times head dimension, not T^3.

question: What does FlashAttention change relative to standard attention?
options: It drops the softmax so that attention becomes linear in sequence length
It only attends to a fixed window of nearby tokens, skipping distant ones
It approximates attention with a low-rank projection of the keys and the values
It computes the same result without storing the full T x T attention matrix
explanation: FlashAttention is exact: it tiles the computation and uses an online softmax so the T x T matrix is never materialized in slow memory. The output is the same as standard attention. Low-rank, linear or sliding-window attention are approximations that change the result.

question: Which two quantities does llmre.training.metrics use to track training throughput?
options: Vocabulary size and the number of BPE merges per second
Held-out perplexity and BLEU score per wall-clock hour
The 6N FLOPs-per-token rule and MFU (model FLOPs utilization)
Global gradient norm and learning rate logged at each step
explanation: llmre.training.metrics provides model_flops_per_token (about 6N for N parameters), tokens_per_step and mfu. MFU compares achieved FLOPs to the hardware's peak. Perplexity and BLEU are quality metrics; gradient norm and LR are optimization diagnostics, not throughput.

question: Which llmre function is the tiled (FlashAttention-style) attention reference?
options: llmre.attention.flash.flash_attention_reference
llmre.evaluation.harness.evaluate_perplexity
llmre.attention.attention.scaled_dot_product_attention
llmre.training.metrics.model_flops_per_token
explanation: flash_attention_reference in llmre.attention.flash is the from-scratch tiled attention implementation, benchmarked by code/scripts/bench_attention.py. scaled_dot_product_attention is the standard attention that materializes the full score matrix, model_flops_per_token counts FLOPs for throughput, and evaluate_perplexity computes a metric.

question: What do scaling laws say about language-model loss?
options: It rises after a fixed number of parameters due to overfitting
It is independent of model size once data is fixed
It falls linearly with the number of parameters without limit
It falls predictably with model size, data and compute
explanation: Scaling laws describe a predictable, power-law decrease of loss as you scale model size, data and compute. It is not linear and does not ignore model size. Even on CPU you can see the shape of the curve by sweeping a size knob.

question: In the capstone's CPU scaling mini-experiment, which knob is swept to see the scaling curve?
options: The tokenizer's vocabulary size
The learning-rate warmup length
The random seed, over many runs
n_embd, over a few model sizes
explanation: code/experiments/scaling_sweep.py sweeps n_embd over a few sizes and plots final loss, keeping corpus, steps and seed fixed. Sweeping seeds measures noise, not scaling, and vocab size or warmup are not model-size knobs.

question: In the capstone scaling sweep, what is the trade-off of a bigger model at a fixed number of steps?
options: It always overfits and must be stopped earlier
It reaches a lower loss but costs more compute per step
It reaches a higher loss and costs less per step
It reaches the same loss at the same cost per step
explanation: With the same steps, a bigger model reaches lower loss, but by the 6ND compute bookkeeping each step costs more (more parameters per token). That is the core scaling trade-off. The other options contradict the observed curve.

question: How is perplexity defined for a held-out set?
options: log(mean cross-entropy) on held-out text
mean(exp(cross-entropy)) over training batches
exp(mean cross-entropy) on held-out text
The fraction of next tokens predicted exactly
explanation: Perplexity is the exponential of the token-averaged cross-entropy on held-out text. It reads as an effective branching factor: a uniform model over V tokens has perplexity V. Accuracy or log of the loss are different quantities, and the measurement must be on held-out data.

question: How does llmre's multiple_choice_score grade a multiple-choice benchmark?
options: By likelihood scoring: comparing length-normalized log-likelihoods of each answer, no weight updates
By fine-tuning the model on the benchmark's training split, then measuring accuracy on the test split
By asking a separate judge model which answer is best, then counting agreement with the gold label
By generating free text for each question and matching the chosen letter with a regular expression
explanation: Likelihood scoring computes the log-likelihood of each candidate answer given the prompt, length-normalized so longer answers are not unfairly penalized, and picks the highest. It requires no training. Fine-tuning on the benchmark would contaminate it; generation-plus-regex and LLM judges are different evaluation styles.

question: Why does llmre's multiple_choice_score use length-normalized log-likelihood?
options: Because normalizing by length converts the log-likelihood into perplexity exactly
Because summed log-likelihood underflows and cannot be computed in float32
Because raw summed log-likelihood penalizes longer answers just for having more tokens
Because longer answers are always correct in multiple-choice benchmarks, so it rewards them
explanation: Each extra token adds a negative log-prob, so summing favors short answers regardless of correctness. Normalizing by length compares answers on a per-token basis. It is not about length being correct, not exactly perplexity, and not a numerical precision issue.

question: What kind of mean does llmre's evaluate_perplexity compute over the cross-entropy?
options: The median of per-token losses across all held-out batches
The maximum per-batch loss, as a worst-case estimate
An unweighted mean of per-batch losses, regardless of how many tokens each batch has
A token-weighted mean, so every token counts equally regardless of batch
explanation: evaluate_perplexity averages cross-entropy weighted by tokens, so batches with more tokens count more and the result equals the true per-token mean. Averaging per-batch means would bias toward small batches. Median or max are not the definition of perplexity.

question: In response-masked SFT, which tokens contribute to the loss?
options: Only the user prompt tokens
Only the special role-delimiter tokens
Only the assistant response tokens
All tokens in the conversation equally
explanation: SFT teaches the model to answer, so the loss is computed on the assistant response only; prompt positions are ignored. Training on the prompt would reward echoing the user. Delimiters alone carry too little signal, though the assistant's closing delimiter is part of the response.

question: In llmre's SFT, what does build_labels write into the prompt positions?
options: 0, so those positions predict the padding token
ignore_index, i.e. -100, so cross-entropy skips them
The end-of-text id, so the model learns to stop
A copy of the input ids, so the prompt is reconstructed
explanation: build_labels sets labels at prompt positions to the sentinel -100 (ignore_index), and masked_cross_entropy drops those positions. Writing 0 or end-of-text would actively train the model to predict those tokens, and copying inputs would train on the prompt.

question: What does a chat template do in llmre's SFT stage?
options: Translates the conversation into a fixed set of intents and slot values for training
Flattens role-tagged messages into one string with delimiters and produces a response mask
Removes the system prompt so that the model sees only the user turns and the assistant replies
Compresses the conversation by summarizing earlier turns so it fits in the context
explanation: render_with_response_mask flattens messages with roles into a single string using delimiters and marks which tokens belong to the assistant response. That mask drives build_labels. It does not translate, drop system prompts, or summarize.

question: Why is the assistant's <|end|> closing delimiter treated as a response token in SFT?
options: So the loss is lower and training converges faster on short replies
So the model learns to stop generating at the end of its answer
So the prompt length can be recovered later from the label tensor
Because special tokens cannot be masked with -100 in cross-entropy
explanation: Including the closer in the trained response tokens teaches the model to emit it, which is how it learns when to stop. If it were masked, the model would never be trained to end its turn and could ramble. Special tokens can be masked; the choice is deliberate.

question: In the capstone's SFT stage, 21 prompt tokens are ignored and 11 response tokens are trained. What would go wrong if all 32 were trained on?
options: The loss would become undefined, because the mean over trained positions divides by zero
The model would be rewarded for echoing the user's prompt, wasting capacity and blurring turns
Nothing would change, because training on all tokens is mathematically equivalent to masking them
The tokenizer would have to be retrained on the prompts so their tokens get their own merges
explanation: Training on prompt tokens rewards the model for echoing the user, wasting capacity on learning to repeat inputs and blurring the 'when is it my turn' signal the chat template teaches. The mechanism that avoids this is ignore_index = -100 in build_labels plus masked_cross_entropy. It is not a numerical issue and is not equivalent to masking.

question: Why is full fine-tuning memory-heavy compared with LoRA?
options: It stores a full copy of the training data in GPU memory
It needs a separate frozen reference model for every single layer
It updates every weight and keeps two AdamW moments per parameter
It recomputes the tokenizer's merges and embeddings at every training step
explanation: Full fine-tuning has gradients and two AdamW moment buffers for every parameter. LoRA freezes the base weights, so only the small adapters carry gradients and optimizer state. Tokenizers and data copies are not the main memory cost.

question: What is the LoRA forward computation for a wrapped linear layer?
options: y = B(A(Wx)), with all three matrices trained
y = (W + A) x, with A trained to full rank
y = alpha * W x + r * B x, with W trained
y = Wx + (alpha/r) * B(Ax), with W frozen
explanation: LoRA keeps the pretrained W frozen and adds a low-rank update B(Ax) scaled by alpha/r. A projects down to rank r and B projects back up. A full-rank additive update or training W defeats the purpose; chaining the matrices multiplicatively changes the base function.

question: How is LoRA's B matrix initialized, and why?
options: To zeros, so the wrapped layer starts identical to the base layer
To the pretrained weights, so the update starts at W
To random normal, so the adapter starts with useful features
To the identity, so the layer doubles its output at init
explanation: With B = 0, the update (alpha/r) * B(Ax) is exactly zero at init, so forward(x) == base(x) and training starts from the pretrained model rather than a perturbed one. The capstone checks this ('identical-to-base at init: True'). A random B would perturb the model immediately.

question: For a LoRA adapter of rank r on a linear layer with input size in and output size out, how many trainable parameters are there?
options: r * in * out
in * out
r * (in + out)
r^2 + in + out
explanation: A has shape (r, in) and B has shape (out, r), giving r*in + r*out = r*(in + out) trainable parameters. in*out is the frozen base weight. For a 64x64 linear at rank 4 that is 4*(64+64) = 512.

question: A LoRA rank-4 adapter on a 64x64 linear reports 512 trainable of 4608 parameters. Where does the 4608 come from?
options: Twice the 512 adapter count plus the 64-dim bias vectors
4096 frozen base weights plus 512 bias and norm terms
512 adapter parameters plus the 4096 frozen base weights (64 x 64)
512 adapter parameters times 9 wrapped linear layers in total
explanation: A is (4, 64) = 256 and B is (64, 4) = 256, so 512 trainable. The frozen base weight is 64*64 = 4096. 512 + 4096 = 4608, so about 11.1% of the parameters are trainable.

question: What does LoRALinear.merge do in llmre?
options: Merges two different LoRA adapters into one by averaging their A and B matrices elementwise
Combines the A and B matrices into a single rank-1 vector to reduce memory
Unfreezes the base weight so that full fine-tuning can resume from the adapter
Folds the low-rank update into the base weight so inference needs no extra compute
explanation: Merging computes W + (alpha/r) * B A and stores it as the layer weight, so the merged layer behaves the same with a single matmul. It does not average adapters, reduce rank, or unfreeze anything. mark_only_lora_trainable is the function that controls which parameters train.

question: What form does preference data take for DPO?
options: For each prompt, a single response with a scalar human rating
For each prompt, a gold answer and a programmatic verifier function
For each prompt, a chosen response y_w and a rejected response y_l
For each response, a list of token-level corrections from annotators
explanation: Alignment starts from pairs: a prompt with a chosen (winning) response y_w and a rejected (losing) response y_l. DPO optimizes directly on these pairs. Scalar ratings or verifiers belong to other setups (reward regression, RLVR).

question: What does DPO avoid compared with the classic RLHF pipeline?
options: Using preference pairs, replacing them with scalar ratings
Using a frozen reference model to anchor the policy's KL
Training a separate reward model and sampling from the policy
Computing sequence log-probabilities under the current policy
explanation: DPO optimizes the policy against preference pairs directly, with no reward model and no sampling. It still uses a frozen reference model and sequence log-probs (sequence_logprob), and it still needs preference pairs.

question: In the DPO derivation, why does the beta * log Z(x) term disappear?
options: It depends only on the prompt, so it cancels in the chosen-minus-rejected difference
It is absorbed into the learning rate, since both scale the gradient by a constant
It is set to zero by choosing beta = 0, which removes the KL term from the objective
It is estimated by sampling completions from the reference and then subtracted out
explanation: The partition-function term beta*log Z(x) is the same for both responses of the same prompt, so it cancels in r(y_w) - r(y_l). That leaves a loss with only the policy and a frozen reference. beta = 0 would remove the KL constraint, and Z is never estimated by sampling.

question: In the classic RLHF path, which loss trains the reward model on preference pairs?
options: The PPO clipped surrogate objective with a KL penalty to the reference
Cross-entropy of the next token on chosen responses only, as in SFT
The Bradley-Terry loss: P(y_w beats y_l) = sigmoid(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l))
Mean squared error between the predicted reward and a human 1-10 score
explanation: The reward model is trained with the Bradley-Terry link: the probability that the chosen response wins is the sigmoid of the reward difference, and the loss is its negative log. PPO's clipped objective is used afterwards to train the policy, not the reward model.

question: In RLHF with PPO, what keeps the policy from drifting too far from the reference model?
options: Removing the clipping from PPO's surrogate objective
A KL penalty to the reference, entering through the reward
Lowering the reward model's learning rate during PPO updates
Freezing the policy's attention layers and training only MLPs
explanation: PPO-based RLHF adds a KL penalty between the policy and the frozen reference, which enters the reward. Together with the clipped objective it limits drift. Freezing layers or adjusting the reward model's LR are not the mechanism, and removing clipping would make updates less stable.

question: How does DPO relate to the reward-model + PPO path?
options: DPO is a preprocessing step that filters the preference pairs before PPO runs on them
DPO is PPO applied to a verifiable reward, with the critic replaced by a group-mean baseline
DPO short-circuits it, optimizing the policy on preference pairs with no reward model or PPO
DPO trains the reward model from the preference pairs, and PPO then trains the policy against it
explanation: The reward model + PPO route is the classic RLHF path that DPO short-circuits: DPO uses the closed-form link between reward and policy/reference log-ratio to skip both the reward model and RL sampling. It is not a PPO preprocessing step, and it does not use verifiable rewards.

section: (12) GRPO + RLVR on a verifiable task
question: What does GRPO drop compared with PPO?
options: The learned critic (value function), using the group's mean reward as baseline
The policy model itself, replacing it with a table of sampled completions per prompt
Sampling multiple completions, scoring a single greedy completion per prompt instead
The clipped importance ratio, taking plain REINFORCE steps on the advantage
explanation: GRPO removes PPO's critic: it samples a group of completions per prompt and uses the group mean reward as the baseline. It keeps a clipped ratio and, by design, relies on sampling multiple completions per prompt.

section: (12) GRPO + RLVR on a verifiable task
question: What is the GRPO advantage for completion i in a group?
options: A_i = (r_i - mean(r)) / std(r)
A_i = r_i - V(x), with V a learned critic
A_i = r_i / max(r)
A_i = log r_i - log mean(r)
explanation: GRPO standardizes rewards within the group: subtract the group mean and divide by the group standard deviation. A learned critic V(x) is PPO's baseline, which GRPO removes. Dividing by the max or taking logs is not the GRPO formula.

section: (12) GRPO + RLVR on a verifiable task
question: Why is a verifiable reward harder to hack than a learned reward model?
options: It uses a larger neural network than the policy, so it is harder to fool
It is evaluated by human raters at every step, who catch gaming quickly
It is a rule that checks the answer (e.g. exact-match), not a learned proxy
It is trained on more preference data than a typical RLHF reward model
explanation: RLVR uses a programmatic check, such as exact-match on arithmetic, so the policy cannot exploit quirks of a learned proxy. A learned reward model can be gamed because it is only an approximation. Verifiers are not trained on preferences and are not human-in-the-loop.

section: (12) GRPO + RLVR on a verifiable task
question: In the capstone's RLVR stage, which verifier is used?
options: llmre.reasoning.verifiers.arithmetic_verifier, exact-match on arithmetic answers
A perplexity threshold on the generated answer under the pretrained capstone GPT
An LLM judge that scores each answer's fluency and correctness on a 1-10 scale
A Bradley-Terry reward model trained on the capstone's DPO preference pairs
explanation: The capstone's RLVR uses arithmetic_verifier, which returns reward based on whether the arithmetic answer exactly matches. That is a rule-based verifiable reward. A reward model or LLM judge would be a learned proxy, and perplexity does not check correctness.

section: (12) GRPO + RLVR on a verifiable task
question: What should you look at in llmre's run_rlvr history to see RL working?
options: The number of LoRA parameters increasing
The correct-rate rising over GRPO steps
The tokenizer's vocabulary size growing
The perplexity on the pretraining corpus rising
explanation: run_rlvr records a history whose key signal is the correct-rate climbing as GRPO updates the policy. In the capstone run it goes from 0.062 to 1.000 over 80 steps. Vocabulary size and LoRA counts don't change, and pretraining perplexity is not the RL signal.

question: What is self-consistency in reasoning?
options: Running the same chain of thought twice with greedy decoding and comparing the two outputs
Checking that the final answer is consistent with the grammar and wording of the prompt
Sampling several chains of thought and taking a majority vote over their final answers
Training the model to agree with its own previous outputs on rephrased versions of a task
explanation: Self-consistency samples multiple reasoning chains and picks the most common final answer. Greedy decoding twice gives identical outputs and no voting benefit. It is an inference-time method, not training the model to agree with itself.

question: What two-stage loop does llmre's mini_r1 implement, following the R1 recipe?
options: Pretraining, then distillation into a smaller tokenizer
DPO first, then tokenizer retraining
RL first, then pretraining from scratch
SFT first, then RL with verifiable rewards
explanation: mini_r1 does an SFT stage then an RL stage with verifiable rewards, mirroring the R1 recipe that trains chain-of-thought behavior in with RLVR. The other orders mix in stages unrelated to the R1 pipeline.

question: In llmre's self_consistency, what property of the majority vote should you look at?
options: Its weighting by answer length
Its random tie-break for diversity
Its deterministic tie-break
Its use of a learned voting network
explanation: The capstone points at the deterministic majority-vote tie-break: when two answers have the same count, the result must not depend on randomness, so runs are reproducible. A learned voter or length weighting are not part of self_consistency.

question: What is chain-of-thought prompting?
options: Chaining several models so each refines the previous output
Feeding the model's answer back as the next prompt until it stops changing
Making the model show its intermediate steps before giving the final answer
Concatenating many examples into one long prompt without instructions
explanation: Chain-of-thought elicits reasoning by having the model write out its steps before the answer (cot_prompt), and extract_answer pulls the final answer out. It is not model chaining or iterative re-prompting.

question: How does a model use a tool in llmre's tool-use stage?
options: It executes Python directly inside the model's forward pass via special tokens
It sends free-text requests to a human operator, who pastes the results back in
It emits a structured call; a runtime runs the real function and feeds the result back
It memorizes tool outputs during pretraining and reproduces them later whenever they are needed
explanation: The model emits a structured tool call, which parse_tool_call parses; the ToolRegistry executes the real function and the result is fed back into the context (run_tool_loop). The model never executes code itself.

question: What does llmre's ToolRegistry do when a tool call raises an exception?
options: Silently retries the call with the same arguments until it eventually succeeds
Crashes the loop on purpose so that the bug is noticed immediately
Turns the exception into a structured error result instead of crashing
Returns an empty string as if the call succeeded, so the model continues
explanation: The registry runs the call and converts any exception into a structured error that is fed back to the model, so the loop keeps going and the model can react. Crashing would kill the agent; silent retries or empty results hide the failure.

question: What does llmre's ToolRegistry advertise to the model about available tools?
options: The Python source code of each tool
Nothing; tools are discovered by trial and error
JSON schemas describing each tool
Example outputs only, without argument descriptions
explanation: The registry advertises JSON schemas for each tool (name, arguments and types), so the model knows how to form a valid call. It does not ship source code or rely on trial and error.

question: How is llmre's built-in calculator tool made safe?
options: It runs Python's eval inside a try/except block that catches every error
It blocks a list of known dangerous function names such as exec and open
It vets the expression's AST against an allow-list of permitted operations
It only accepts expressions shorter than a fixed length with no letters
explanation: The calculator parses the expression and checks the AST against an allow-list, so only explicitly permitted nodes run. A block-list can always miss something dangerous, and wrapping eval in try/except gives no security. Length limits do not prevent malicious code.

question: What loop does a ReAct agent run?
options: Action -> Reward -> Gradient step, repeated on every turn until the reward converges
Thought -> Action -> Observation, until a final answer or the step budget runs out
Plan -> Execute all steps -> Report, with no observations read between the steps
Retrieve -> Generate -> Rerank, for a fixed three steps per question and no tools
explanation: ReAct interleaves reasoning (Thought), tool calls (Action) and results (Observation) until a final answer or the step budget runs out. Planning everything without observations loses feedback; retrieve-generate-rerank is RAG; reward-gradient loops are RL training.

question: What turns llmre's ReAct loop into a mini SWE-agent?
options: Training it with DPO on code preferences
Removing the step budget so it can run indefinitely
Replacing the model with a larger pretrained checkpoint
Wrapping it with a small file view/edit/run interface
explanation: llmre.agents.swe_agent.solve wraps the ReAct loop with tools to view, edit and run files, which makes it a mini software-engineering agent. Model size, DPO, or removing the step budget do not give it the file interface.

question: Why is llmre's run_react described as tool-registry-agnostic?
options: It hard-codes a fixed calculator and search tool
It ignores tool results and only uses the model's thoughts
Tools are injected into it, never imported by it
It can only call tools defined in the same file
explanation: run_react receives its tools as an argument (dependency injection), so any registry can be plugged in. Hard-coding or importing specific tools would couple it to one setup. It does use tool results as Observations.

question: To claim a change caused an improvement, what must an ablation do?
options: Vary several things at once to save compute
Vary exactly one thing and hold everything else fixed
Change the seed along with the change to average out noise
Compare against a published number from a different setup
explanation: Attribution requires one independent variable with everything else as controls. If two things change, you cannot tell which one caused the effect. Comparing to a different setup confounds harness, data and budget differences.

question: In the capstone's scaling sweep used as an ablation template, what is held fixed?
options: Only the seed; the corpus and step count vary with the model size
The corpus, the number of steps and the seed; only n_embd changes
Only n_embd; the corpus, steps and seed are randomized per run
Nothing; all knobs change together to explore the whole space
explanation: The scaling sweep keeps the same corpus, same steps and same seed and changes only n_embd. That is the 'one independent variable, everything else a control' pattern. Letting other knobs vary would confound the comparison.

question: Where are the reproducible knobs of the capstone run stored?
options: Hard-coded inside the GPT class
In code/configs/capstone.yaml
In environment variables set by the shell
In code/reports/capstone_report.md
explanation: The driver reads code/configs/capstone.yaml (model size, steps, LR, seed) so the run is reproducible. The report is the output, not the config, and hard-coding or environment variables would make the run harder to reproduce.

question: You want to claim 'RMSNorm lowers final loss vs LayerNorm.' What must be true of the runs?
options: Both runs use a single seed each and identical settings, and whichever reaches the lower loss wins
Only the norm changes, everything else is fixed, with mean +/- std over seeds compared to seed noise
The RMSNorm run gets more steps and a retuned learning rate to compensate for being the newer method
Each run uses whichever learning rate gives it the lowest loss, with the other knobs left free to vary
explanation: Change exactly one thing (the norm), hold corpus, tokens, steps, seeds, size, optimizer and LR schedule fixed, and run several seeds. Report mean +/- std and check whether confidence intervals overlap. A single seed cannot separate effect from noise, and giving one run extra steps confounds the result.

question: What is the deliverable of a research experiment, according to the capstone?
options: A slide deck summarizing the best results across all runs
The trained model checkpoint, uploaded with its config file
A loss-curve screenshot comparing the final runs side by side
A report a colleague can reproduce, not the model itself
explanation: The capstone states the deliverable is a report someone else can reproduce: QUESTION, HYPOTHESIS, METHOD, BASELINE, VARIABLES, RESULTS, ANALYSIS, LIMITATIONS, CONCLUSION, NEXT. A checkpoint or chart without method, baseline and limitations is not reproducible evidence.

question: Which sections make up the llmre experiment report template?
options: SUMMARY / CONTEXT / METRICS / LEADERBOARD / DISCUSSION / RISKS / ROADMAP / OWNERS / TIMELINE
QUESTION / HYPOTHESIS / METHOD / BASELINE / VARIABLES / RESULTS / ANALYSIS / LIMITATIONS / CONCLUSION / NEXT
GOAL / SETUP / CODE / DATA / OUTPUT / METRICS / ISSUES / FIXES / DONE
ABSTRACT / INTRODUCTION / RELATED WORK / METHOD / EXPERIMENTS / DISCUSSION / CONCLUSION / REFERENCES
explanation: code/reports/EXPERIMENT_TEMPLATE.md has QUESTION, HYPOTHESIS, METHOD, BASELINE, VARIABLES, RESULTS, ANALYSIS, LIMITATIONS, CONCLUSION and NEXT. That structure forces a falsifiable question, a baseline and stated limitations. Paper-style sections lack the baseline and variables discipline.

question: Where does the capstone driver write its filled-in experiment report?
options: code/reports/capstone_report.md
code/tests/test_capstone.py
code/configs/capstone.yaml
code/reports/EXPERIMENT_TEMPLATE.md
explanation: The driver fills in the template and writes code/reports/capstone_report.md. EXPERIMENT_TEMPLATE.md is the blank template, capstone.yaml is the input config, and test_capstone.py is the smoke test.

question: Which stages does the capstone driver code/scripts/capstone.py actually run?
options: A tiny version of stages (1)-(9) and (12): tokenizer through LoRA, plus GRPO/RLVR
Only the post-training stages (SFT, LoRA, DPO, PPO, GRPO) on a downloaded checkpoint
Only pretraining and evaluation, leaving every post-training stage to separate scripts
All 17 stages at full scale, including PPO, tool use, ReAct agents and the SWE-agent
explanation: The driver runs a tiny end-to-end version of stages 1-9 (tokenizer, GPT, pretraining, data, profiling notes, scaling, eval, SFT, LoRA) and stage 12 (GRPO + RLVR), then writes the report. Stages like PPO, tool use and agents are covered by their own entry points but not run by the driver.

question: In the capstone run, pretraining loss falls from 5.935 to 0.067 nats and held-out perplexity is 1.07. What does that indicate?
options: The model generalizes far beyond GPT-2 quality on this held-out text
The tiny model memorized the tiny corpus, the expected smoke-test outcome
The loss is miscomputed, because perplexity can never fall below 2
The tokenizer collapsed so that every document maps to a single token
explanation: The corpus is a dozen repeated sentences, so a tiny model memorizes it and perplexity drops near 1. That proves the pipeline learns but says nothing about quality. Perplexity can be any value at least 1, and nothing indicates tokenizer collapse.

question: In the capstone run, what is the uniform-baseline perplexity that the 1.07 result is compared to?
options: About 256, the byte count
About 374, the vocabulary size
About 1.0, the minimum possible
About 2.72, the value of e
explanation: A uniform model over V tokens has perplexity V, and the capstone vocabulary is about 373-374 tokens (256 bytes + 117 merges plus specials), so the baseline is about 374. Perplexity 1 is the floor, and 256 is only the byte base.

question: In the capstone run, RLVR lifts the arithmetic correct-rate from 0.062 to 1.000. Why is 0.062 described as near chance?
options: It is the fraction of prompt tokens in each RL batch
It equals 1/16, the reciprocal of the GRPO group size
It is close to the ~1/10 expected from a 10-way answer space
It equals the learning rate used for the GRPO policy updates
explanation: With about 10 possible answers, a random policy would be right about 1/10 of the time, so 0.062 is near chance before training. RL then drives it to 1.000. It is not a group size, token fraction or learning rate.

question: What do the capstone's two learning signals, which a smoke test exists to check, consist of?
options: Loss going down and correct-rate going up
Vocabulary size going up and merge count going down
Learning rate going up and gradient norm going down
Throughput going up and memory going down
explanation: A smoke test checks that the pipeline actually learns: pretraining/SFT loss decreases and the RLVR correct-rate increases. code/tests/test_capstone.py asserts exactly this at even smaller size. Throughput or vocabulary changes say nothing about learning.

question: What does code/tests/test_capstone.py assert?
options: That loss falls and correct-rate rises, at even smaller size than the driver
That the whole run finishes in under one second on a single GPU
That held-out perplexity matches GPT-2 small's published value on WikiText
That every module's output is bit-identical to a stored reference tensor
explanation: test_capstone.py checks the two learning signals (loss down, correct-rate up) on an even smaller configuration. It does not compare against GPT-2, timing, or bit-exact references.

question: Why should a memorization perplexity like 1.07 never be quoted as a quality result?
options: Because perplexity is only well defined for runs done on GPU hardware
It only shows the pipeline can learn a repeated tiny corpus, not that it generalizes
Because the value is below the theoretical minimum perplexity of 2 for any model
Because perplexity is not a valid language-model metric for byte-level tokenizers
explanation: The low value comes from memorizing a dozen repeated sentences. It is a correct smoke-test outcome and a deliberate limitation stated in the report, but quality claims need a large, varied corpus and genuinely held-out data. Perplexity is a valid metric, its minimum is 1, and it is hardware independent.

question: Why does the capstone use a categorical policy table for RLVR instead of the pretrained GPT?
options: Because GRPO cannot be applied to transformer policies, only to tabular ones
Because the pretrained GPT has no output distribution over the possible answers
Speed and clarity on CPU: the GRPO update is identical; the table isolates RL from generation
Because verifiable rewards only work with tabular policies that enumerate every answer
explanation: GRPO's algorithm (sample a group, standardize rewards, clipped policy-gradient step) is the same for a lookup table or a GPT emitting answer tokens. The table makes the correct-rate visibly climb in under a second. Swapping in the GPT changes the engineering (sampling token sequences), not the update rule, which is why it is the report's next experiment.

question: What hardware does a real GPT-2 small (124M) pretrain need, per the capstone's hardware track?
options: 1x A100/H100 (40-80 GB), tens of GPU-hours for a few billion tokens; CPU-only is not feasible
A cluster of 1,000 H100 GPUs for about a month, the same as a frontier pretraining run
A single 8 GB consumer GPU for about ten minutes, using LoRA instead of full training
A laptop CPU for about an hour, since 124M parameters fit easily in system memory
explanation: A GPT-2 small pretrain is estimated at tens of GPU-hours on one A100/H100, using about 15-30 GB with mixed precision and gradient accumulation. CPU-only is not feasible. A month on 1,000 GPUs is frontier scale, not 124M.

question: Why can LoRA fit a 7B model on a single 24 GB consumer GPU while full SFT of the same model needs multiple 40-80 GB GPUs?
options: LoRA quantizes the activations and gradients to one bit, so memory falls by roughly 16x overall
LoRA trains on far fewer tokens than full SFT, so it needs a much smaller activation buffer
LoRA skips the forward pass through frozen layers, so their activations are never stored
With LoRA, optimizer state covers only the small adapters; full SFT keeps it for every weight
explanation: LoRA's frozen base needs no gradients or optimizer moments, so only the adapters carry that state. Full SFT stores gradients plus two AdamW moments for all 7B parameters. LoRA still runs the full forward pass and does not inherently change token count or quantize activations.

question: How does the compute cost of DPO compare to SFT?
options: Roughly the same as SFT: two forward passes, the policy and a frozen reference
Identical to PPO, because both train a critic alongside the policy each step
Much cheaper, because DPO skips the backward pass and only scores pairs
Far heavier, because DPO samples fresh completions from the policy every step
explanation: DPO costs about the same as SFT, plus a forward pass through the frozen reference, and needs no sampling. PPO/GRPO are far heavier because they generate completions every step. DPO does train with backward passes and does not use a critic.

question: In PPO/GRPO with real generation, what usually dominates cost?
options: Generating (sampling) completions, not the gradient step
Writing full optimizer-state checkpoints to disk each step
The KL penalty computation over the full vocabulary
The tokenizer's encode step on every sampled completion
explanation: Generation-based RL samples completions every step, so sampling dominates cost. Budget several GPUs and hours-to-days even for a small model. Tokenization and KL computation are cheap, and checkpointing is not the bottleneck.

question: What makes frontier reasoning RL runs cost thousands of GPU-hours?
options: Long chains of thought make each rollout long, so sampling at scale is costly; same mechanism as the toy
They must retrain the tokenizer on every RL step, as the vocabulary drifts with the reasoning traces
They require a full pretraining pass between RL steps to keep the policy from forgetting language
They use a completely different algorithm from GRPO, which needs a learned critic per token
explanation: The mechanism is identical to the toy loop; only the scale of sampling changes. Long chain-of-thought rollouts make each sample expensive. It is not a different algorithm, and no tokenizer retraining or re-pretraining is involved.

question: What is the Chinchilla rule of thumb for a compute-optimal pretrain?
options: About 1 token per parameter
About 20 tokens per parameter
About 200 tokens per parameter
About 2 tokens per FLOP
explanation: The Chinchilla rule of thumb (reasonable industry practice) is about 20 training tokens per parameter for compute-optimal pretraining. 1 or 200 tokens per parameter would be badly under- or over-trained for compute optimality, and tokens per FLOP is not a meaningful ratio here.

question: How should the tokenizer's vocabulary size be scaled up from the toy capstone driver?
options: Toward 32k-50k tokens
Toward 256 tokens, the byte count
Toward 1 million tokens
It should stay at the toy size of about 373
explanation: To grow the tokenizer stage, raise tokenizer.vocab_size toward 32k-50k, typical of GPT-2-class models. 256 would be bytes only, 1M would bloat embeddings, and the toy size is only for the smoke test.

question: Which of these is part of scaling up the capstone pipeline from the toy driver?
options: Disable gradient clipping so that larger models are not slowed down by small updates
Replace the BPE tokenizer with a character-level one so that the vocabulary stays small
Use a real filtered, decontaminated corpus and move to a GPU with mixed precision and FlashAttention
Keep the toy corpus but train for millions of steps, so the model sees every sentence many times
explanation: Scaling up means a real corpus (filtered and decontaminated, Module 11), a bigger model toward GPT-2 sizes, and GPU training with mixed precision and FlashAttention (Module 8). Training longer on the toy corpus just memorizes it further; dropping clipping or BPE are not recommended steps.

question: What does the capstone report name as the next experiment for the RLVR stage?
options: Replacing the arithmetic verifier with a learned reward model trained on preferences
Removing the group sampling so that each GRPO step needs only one completion
Replacing the categorical RLVR policy with the GPT itself emitting answer tokens
Replacing GRPO with supervised fine-tuning on the correct arithmetic answers
explanation: The natural next step is to have the pretrained GPT generate answer tokens as the RLVR policy, instead of the categorical lookup table. That changes the engineering, not the GRPO update. A learned reward model would reintroduce hackability, and removing group sampling breaks GRPO's baseline.

question: According to the course's readiness matrix, when is a skill rated 'Advanced'?
options: When you have read the relevant paper once and can summarize its main contribution
When you have used it in a production framework such as HF, TRL or DeepSpeed at work
When you can explain, derive, implement, test, benchmark, debug and relate it to a paper
When you can run the provided script without errors and reproduce its printed numbers
explanation: Advanced means the full chain: explain -> derive -> implement -> test -> benchmark -> debug -> relate-to-a-paper, from memory. Reading or running something once, or using a framework, covers only part of that chain.

question: What should a write-up of your own experiment contain, following the capstone report's model?
options: One falsifiable question, real numbers with a baseline, and stated limitations
Several open-ended questions and qualitative impressions of how the runs went
Only the best result across all runs and seeds, presented without a baseline
A detailed description of the code changes, without any measured numbers
explanation: One report, one falsifiable question, real numbers compared to a baseline, and stated limitations, just like code/reports/capstone_report.md. Cherry-picking the best result or omitting numbers makes the report non-reproducible and non-falsifiable.

question: Why is OLMo 2 suggested as a strong first paper after finishing the course?
options: It is the largest open model ever trained, so it defines the current frontier
It uses no transformer components, so it contrasts well with what you built
It requires no GPU to reproduce, so you can rerun its full training run on a laptop
Its data, code and checkpoints are fully open, so you can reproduce and ablate it
explanation: OLMo 2 is fully open (data, code, checkpoints), so you can reproduce it and ablate it against your own llmre implementation. It is not the largest model, it is a transformer, and reproducing it still needs serious GPUs.

question: What loop is described as 'the job' of a research engineer at the end of the course?
options: Download, fine-tune, deploy, repeat
Brainstorm, prototype, ship, market
Read, implement, test, measure, write
Benchmark, tweak hyperparameters, publish the best seed
explanation: After reading a paper with the nine-question method, implement its change inside llmre, wire it into the capstone, measure, and write it up with the experiment template. Publishing the best seed is the anti-pattern the ablation discipline warns against.

question: When reading a new paper after the course, what should you do with the one thing it changes?
options: Implement it in llmre, wire it into code/scripts/capstone.py, and write it up with the template
Download the authors' released checkpoint and report their numbers alongside your baseline
Summarize it in a blog post with its key equations, without running any code yourself
Add it to every stage of the pipeline at once, so its full effect is measured in one run
explanation: The suggested workflow is to implement the paper's single change inside llmre, run it through the capstone driver, and write a report. Re-reporting authors' numbers is not reproduction, and changing every stage at once would break the one-variable ablation discipline.
